prompt: What is a SwiftUI view, such as `CourseListView`?
hint: It is a struct.

choices.text: An object that lives on the screen until it is removed
choices.why: That is the picture from other toolkits; here nothing on the screen is yours to keep.

choices.text: A small value describing part of the screen
choices.why: Right: SwiftUI reads it and keeps the real thing elsewhere.

choices.text: A pointer to the pixels SwiftUI drew
choices.why: A view holds data and a body, no pixels.

choices.text: A class SwiftUI subclasses for each screen
choices.why: Views are structs; nothing subclasses them.

prompt: A view declares `var taps = 0` as a plain stored property and adds one on each tap. What does the person see?
hint: When is the struct created again?

choices.text: The count, kept for as long as the app runs
choices.why: A plain property lives only as long as that copy of the struct.

choices.text: The count, but only on an iPad
choices.why: The platform does not change what a struct remembers.

choices.text: A count that is lost whenever the parent's body runs again
choices.why: Right: the view is created again from scratch; what it must remember goes in `@State`, lesson 6.

choices.text: A crash, because views are immutable
choices.why: Nothing crashes. A struct method could not even assign it without `mutating`, but the point is the reset.

prompt: Why is it fine that a list of fifty rows creates fifty view structs every time it is described?
hint: What does creating one cost?

choices.text: A view is a few bytes of description, cheap to make
choices.why: Right: the expensive objects stay with SwiftUI.

choices.text: SwiftUI reuses the same fifty structs by reference, without copying them
choices.why: Structs are values; there are no references to reuse.

choices.text: Only the visible rows are ever created
choices.why: That is a lazy container's behaviour, lesson 8, and not the reason here.

choices.text: The compiler turns them into one view
choices.why: The builder combines them into one value, but each is still made.

prompt: Why did `swift opaque.swift` refuse `header(short:)`?
hint: Read the two notes under the error.

choices.text: `Card` has no `render()` for `Minutes`
choices.why: `Minutes` implements `render()`; the conformance is fine.

choices.text: `some Card` promised one type and the returns gave two
choices.why: Right: `Minutes` on one path and `Title` on the other.

choices.text: `some` is only allowed on a SwiftUI body
choices.why: Opaque types are a Swift feature; this file has no SwiftUI.

choices.text: A function with `if` cannot return a protocol
choices.why: With one type on both paths it compiles, `if` and all.

prompt: With what exit status did `swift opaque.swift; echo $?` end?
hint: The last line of the capture.

prompt: A body wraps each branch of an `if` in `AnyView` to make it compile. According to Apple's documentation, what happens each time the condition flips?
hint: The wrapped type changes.

choices.text: Nothing, because `AnyView` has the same type whichever view it wraps
choices.why: Its own type is the same; the documentation is about the wrapped type changing.

choices.text: The old hierarchy is destroyed and a new one created
choices.why: Right, which is the cost of hiding the structure SwiftUI compares by.

choices.text: The compiler rejects the body as in `opaque.swift`
choices.why: Type erasure is exactly what makes it compile.

choices.text: SwiftUI caches both branches and swaps them
choices.why: The documentation describes destroying and creating, not caching.

prompt: Where should a view start downloading the courses, given that its body runs many times?
hint: A modifier made for work that starts with a view.

choices.text: At the top of `body`, before the `List`
choices.why: That would start a download every time the body runs.

choices.text: In the view's `init`
choices.why: The struct is created again often; init runs each time.

choices.text: In a `.task` modifier
choices.why: Right: lesson 12 uses it, and it is cancelled if the view goes away.

choices.text: In a computed property the body reads
choices.why: It runs whenever the body reads it, which is the same problem.

prompt: Match each change to the lesson that makes it ask a body again.
hint: Section 04's table.

pairs.left: A value the parent passed in
A property of an observable model the body read

prompt: A body sorts the plan's thousand sessions by date every time it runs. What is the problem, and where does the sort belong?
hint: How many times does a body run, and who decides?

choices.text: None: a body runs once, so the sort runs once
choices.why: A body runs whenever its inputs may have changed.

choices.text: It repeats on every run; sort where the data changes, or in the model
choices.why: Right: SwiftUI decides how often the body runs, so the body must be cheap.

choices.text: Sorting is not allowed in SwiftUI; use the server
choices.why: Sorting is allowed anywhere; the issue is how often.

choices.text: It changes the order of rows on screen, so move it to `.task`
choices.why: `.task` is for asynchronous work that starts with a view, not for a derived order.

prompt: `bodies.swift` drew four frames. How many times did the body run?
hint: Count the lines that say `body run`.

prompt: Why did the third frame of `bodies.swift` print `nothing to redo`?
hint: What changed before it, and did the body read it?

choices.text: `notes` is not marked `@Observable`
choices.why: The macro marks the class, and `notes` is observed like the others.

choices.text: The second frame already drew the change
choices.why: The change to `notes` happened after the second frame.

choices.text: The body never read `notes`
choices.why: Right: only a change to what was read calls `onChange`.

choices.text: An empty string does not count as a change
choices.why: `notes` went from empty to `bring the book`, which is a change.

prompt: In `Screen.frame()`, suppose the body read `model.notes` only when `model.minutes > 55`. After `model.minutes = 60` and a frame, would a change to `notes` then run the body?
hint: Tracking records what a run actually read.

choices.text: Yes, because that run read `notes`
choices.why: Right: each run records its own reads, so the set changes with the data.

choices.text: No, because the first run did not read `notes`
choices.why: Tracking is redone on every run; the first run's set is gone.

choices.text: No, because conditions inside a body are not tracked
choices.why: Whatever the closure reads is tracked, conditions included.

choices.text: Only if `notes` is read before `minutes`
choices.why: Order does not matter; what is read is recorded.

prompt: The function that runs a closure and records every observable property it reads is `withObservation___`.
hint: The word that means following something.

prompt: In `card(title:minutes:done:)`, why does the second card have only two lines?
hint: `done` was false.

choices.text: `buildBlock` drops the last line of every block
choices.why: The first card kept all three lines.

choices.text: The `if` was false, so `buildOptional` got `nil` and gave nothing
choices.why: Right: an `if` with no `else` adds nothing when false.

choices.text: Mobile Fundamentals has no minutes
choices.why: It shows `40 min`; the missing line is `done`.

choices.text: The builder runs the function twice and keeps the shorter result
choices.why: The compiler rewrites the function once, before it runs.

prompt: Match each builder function to the code it handles.
hint: Section 06's `LinesBuilder`.

pairs.right: Each bare line, turned into a part
All the parts of a block, joined into one value

prompt: When does the rewriting of a builder function into `buildBlock` and `buildOptional` calls happen?
hint: Nothing special happened at run time.

choices.text: Each time the function runs, by Swift's runtime
choices.why: The runtime calls the builder's functions; it does not write them in.

choices.text: At compile time
choices.why: Right: the compiler rewrites the body before anything runs.

choices.text: When SwiftUI first draws the view
choices.why: `builder.swift` has no SwiftUI and was still rewritten.

choices.text: Only in Xcode 27, with `ContentBuilder`
choices.why: Result builders have worked this way since before Xcode 27, on Linux too.

prompt: `branches.swift` printed the types of `row(done: true)` and `row(done: false)`. What did it show?
hint: Both lines of the type are in the capture.

choices.text: `Pair<Text, Image>` and `Pair<Text, Text>`
choices.why: Then `some Any` would have refused, as in section 03.

choices.text: The same type twice
choices.why: Right: `Pair<Text, Either<Image, Text>>`; the branch is in the value.

choices.text: `Either<Image, Text>` alone, without the title
choices.why: The title is the first slot of the `Pair`.

choices.text: `Any`, because the return type is `some Any`
choices.why: `type(of:)` prints the concrete type hidden behind `some`.

prompt: `CourseDetailView` shows a note field inside `if done { … } else { … }`, the same field in both branches with a different colour. Someone types half a note and `done` flips. What happens, and what is the fix?
hint: The two branches are two views.

choices.text: The text moves to the other field, since both are the same type
choices.why: Same type in two slots is still two identities.

choices.text: Nothing, because SwiftUI compares the fields by their text
choices.why: Identity here comes from the slot, not from the content.

choices.text: The half note is lost; use one field whose colour depends on `done`
choices.why: Right: one view with a changing value keeps its identity.

choices.text: The app crashes, since a text field cannot be destroyed while someone is typing in it
choices.why: It is destroyed quietly, which is why the loss surprises.

prompt: Identity given by a view's position in the body's type is called ___ identity.
hint: Lesson 8 sets explicit identity beside it.

prompt: Put the steps in the order `Screen.frame()` follows when the screen is dirty.
hint: Section 05's fourth part.

prompt: Which of these ran on Linux for this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Single files with no SwiftUI.

choices.text: `builder.swift`
choices.why: Yes: a result builder is plain Swift.

choices.text: `bodies.swift`, with `import Observation`
choices.why: Yes: Observation ships with Swift on Linux.

choices.text: `MyView`, the documentation's `View` example
choices.why: No: it imports SwiftUI.

choices.text: A body counted by SwiftUI's own tracking
choices.why: No: section 05 played SwiftUI's part by hand.

prompt: A body returns `Text` when a list is empty and `List` otherwise, using `if`/`else`. Why does it compile when `header(short:)` did not?
hint: What marks `body` and not `header`?

choices.text: `View` accepts two types in a body where `Card` accepts one
choices.why: `some View` is one type, the same rule as `some Card`.

choices.text: SwiftUI wraps every body in `AnyView` for you
choices.why: No: that would throw away the structure SwiftUI compares by.

choices.text: The body's builder turns the `if`/`else` into one type
choices.why: Right, as `ShapeBuilder` did with `Either`.

choices.text: `header` used `return`, and bodies are not allowed to
choices.why: A body with one expression may use `return`; the difference is the builder.
